title: 8 Western Classics Every Educated Person Should Read (Part 2)
author: The Western Spirit
summary: This is Part 2 of The Western Spirit's ongoing series curating essential works of Western civilization. Following an installment covering a first set of 8 classics, the curator (writing under the newsletter name 'The Western Spirit') introduces a second group of 8 canonical texts spanning epic poetry, philosophy, history, and theology: Virgil's Aeneid (Rome's founding epic, written under Augustus and later the core school text of medieval and Renaissance Europe), Plato's Republic (the foundational work of Western political philosophy, built around Socrates's inquiry into justice and the ordered soul), Augustine's Confessions (the first great spiritual autobiography, tracing Augustine's restless search for truth through rhetoric, Manichaeism, and Neoplatonism to Christian conversion), Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy (composed in prison awaiting execution, and among the most-read books of the Middle Ages), Cicero's On Duties (a practical handbook of moral and civic duty written in the last months of Cicero's life), Thucydides's History of the Peloponnesian War (the first analytically rigorous history of the West, studied by Hobbes and the American Founders), Marcus Aurelius's Meditations (a Roman emperor's private stoic notebook on duty and self-command), and Beowulf (the earliest major work of English literature, fusing pagan heroic values with Christian fatalism). For each work the curator gives brief historical/editorial context - who wrote it, when, and why it endured - followed by two to three verbatim quotations from standard English translations. The editorial framing throughout emphasizes continuity: each book is presented as a load-bearing text that shaped later Western thought, from medieval universities to the American Founders to modern soldiers and statesmen. The email closes with a subscriber pitch and a plug for the newsletter's paid 'Athenaeum Book Club,' which was about to begin a read-along of Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov.
points: Virgil's Aeneid frames the founding of Rome itself as an act of toil and sacrifice, memorialized in the underworld line that 'to recall thy steps and pass out to the upper air, this is the task, this the toil.'
Plato's Republic locates justice not in law but in the soul's internal order, arguing the just man 'sets in order his own inner life, and is his own master and his own law.'

Augustine's Confessions, the first true spiritual autobiography, reframes the created world's beauty as a distraction from God rather than a good in itself: 'You were with me, and I was not with you.'
Boethius wrote the Consolation of Philosophy from a prison cell awaiting execution, concluding that 'all fortune is good fortune' because it either rewards, disciplines, punishes, or corrects.
Thucydides's cold-eyed realism in the Peloponnesian War, distilled in 'the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must,' became required reading for Hobbes and the American Founders.
quotes: Perhaps one day it will be a joy to remember even these things.
The just man does not permit the several elements within him to interfere with one another, or any of them to do the work of others.
You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.
Nothing is miserable unless you think it so; and on the other hand, nothing brings happiness unless you are content with it.
We are not born for ourselves alone, but our country claims a share of our being, and our friends a share.
The strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.
You have power over your mind - not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength.
Behaviour that's admired is the path to power among people everywhere.
